summary: Reports on how well existing standards-track MIBs apply to managing World Wide Web servers. It was produced after a BOF at an IETF meeting and is informational.

eli5.summary: People asked whether existing gauges can monitor web servers. This note gives the answer.

subtitle: How to apply existing network management standards to monitor and control web servers.

tldr.problem: Organizations running web servers want to manage them with the same SNMP tools used for network devices, but it is unclear which existing MIBs (Management Information Base modules) apply and what additional attributes are needed.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC examines existing standards-track MIBs (MIB-II, Host Resources, Network Services Monitoring, and Application MIBs) and shows which apply to web servers, then identifies gaps where additional attributes must be defined for comprehensive web server management.
tldr.outcome: Implementers understand the landscape of management standards for web servers and can design management solutions that integrate web servers into enterprise SNMP management, with both operational (host) and service-level monitoring.

facts.label: Existing MIBs analyzed
facts.value: 4 (MIB-II, Host Resources, Network Services Monitoring, Application)

today: RFC 2039 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It documents the state of web server management standardization in 1996 and provides guidance that remains relevant for understanding how to integrate web server management into an SNMP-based infrastructure. Later work extended and formalized HTTP MIB modules based on the requirements and framework outlined here.

sections.title: Managing Web Servers Like Network Devices
sections.content:
By the mid-1990s, organizations deployed many web servers and needed a way to monitor them. They already used SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) with MIBs (Management Information Base modules) to manage network devices like routers and switches. The natural question was: can we use SNMP to manage web servers too?

RFC 2039 was produced following an HTTP-MIB BOF (Birds of a Feather meeting) at IETF meeting 35, at the request of the Network Management Area Director. It surveys what existing management standards can do for web servers and identifies where new standards are needed.
sections.eli5: Managers use special tools to check on network equipment. This RFC asks: can we use the same tools to check on web servers?

sections.title: Two Ways to Monitor a Web Server
sections.content:
The RFC identifies two complementary perspectives on web server management:

The Operational Model views a web server as a computer with hardware, disk space, an operating system, and web server software. Managers in this view care about CPU utilization, disk space, network bandwidth, and whether processes are running. They monitor the host as a whole.

The Service Model views the web server as a black box that responds to client requests. Managers in this view care about how many requests the server handles, whether it is responding quickly, what documents are being served, and what the configuration is. They monitor the service delivered to users.

The two models are orthogonal: an operator may need one view or the other, or both. Management standards should support either model independently.
sections.eli5: You can think about a web server in two ways: as a computer (with memory, disk, power) or as a service (how many requests it handles, how fast it responds). Managers need to watch both.

sections.title: What Existing MIBs Provide
sections.content:
MIB-II defines managed objects for TCP/IP-based devices. For web servers, the applicable groups are System, Interfaces, TCP, UDP, ICMP, and SNMP. This covers basic network and host information.

Host Resources MIB provides uniform objects for managing host computers: system information, storage (disk), devices (including processors and network interfaces), and running/installed software. It is designed for any operating system and captures the Operational Model view. However, it includes mandatory and optional groups, and the dependencies between them can be complex.

Network Services Monitoring MIB defines general-purpose attributes for applications that provide network services, from the service perspective. It includes an applications table (tracking active services) and an associations table (tracking individual client connections). This fits the Service Model well and applies directly to web servers.

Application MIB (sysApplMib) captures installed applications and running processes, including configuration, startup, and history. It relates to Host Resources but addresses some of its shortcomings, like tracking which executable files and configuration files belong to which application.

Together, these MIBs provide significant coverage, but gaps remain for web-server-specific requirements.
sections.eli5: There are already four MIB standards that can tell you about computers, their network equipment, running programs, and network services. Most of what you need is already there.

sections.title: What Is Missing
sections.content:
The existing MIBs do not fully address several important requirements:

Mapping between operational and service views: Neither MIB-II nor the existing MIBs define how to link a running web server process (Operational Model) to the service it provides (Service Model). Managers need to understand this relationship.

Web-specific service metrics: Extensions are needed to track web-server-specific information like request rates, response times, HTTP status codes, and document access statistics that go beyond the generic Network Services Monitoring MIB.

Document management: Statistics about static and dynamic documents served, access permissions, and document freshness are not covered.

Configuration and control: Mechanisms to remotely configure web servers and control them (start, stop, reload configuration, rotate logs) are not fully standardized.

Error reporting: Web servers typically use unstructured log files. There is no standard SNMP mechanism for web server error reporting and logging.

Additional MIB attributes are needed at the top of these standard stacks to create a complete web-server management framework.
sections.eli5: The existing tools can see the host and the service, but they do not connect them. They also do not cover some things managers really want to know about web servers, like how many requests come in and what documents are being served.

sections.title: Building a Web Server Management Standard
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that a complete web server management solution should:

Start with the existing four MIB modules as a foundation. Implement the ones that apply to your management needs (Operational, Service, or both).

Define the relationship between the Network Services Monitoring MIB and the Application MIB so that managers can trace a request from the service level down to the specific processes and host resources involved. This relationship should be general enough to apply to other network services too.

Add web-server-specific MIB extensions on top of the existing standards, covering statistics, configuration, control, and error management. These extensions should be modular so that different levels of management detail can be implemented independently.

The author notes that a standardized approach prevents duplicated work and allows management applications from different vendors to control web servers from multiple vendors in a uniform way. Extensions to this work could eventually cover other information retrieval services like FTP, Gopher, NNTP, and proxies.
sections.eli5: To manage web servers well, start with what already exists, add a few connecting pieces, and build specialized tools on top for web servers specifically.
